partner_context.their_ambition: Aruba, Curaçao and Bonaire — the Dutch Caribbean 'ABC' trio — sit together at ~12°N off the Venezuelan coast, below the main Atlantic hurricane track. Three islands within sight of one another, each a distinct premium draw: Aruba's high-rise resort strip and top-tier cruise calls, Curaçao's UNESCO waterfront and deep-water marinas, and Bonaire, a world dive capital wrapped in a national marine park. The shared ambition is to grow high-value, low-impact tourism without choking the reefs and lagoons in diesel wake and noise.
partner_context.their_pressure: Today the trio is a cluster on the map but not on the water. Inter-island movement runs on costly 19-seat turboprops (Divi Divi, EZ Air) and slow ferries; cruise pax and resort guests transfer by diesel shuttle and taxi; and Bonaire's marine park penalizes exactly the loud, oily craft that serve it. The islands are minutes apart by sea yet linked as if they were an ocean apart.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier turns the ABC trio into a single silent, fast, zero-emission foiling network — the grounded Curaçao↔Bonaire spine and intra-island cruise/airport/resort/dive transfers now, with an aspirational Quanta-LR reach to Aruba. Below the hurricane belt, a fixed foiling fleet earns revenue 12 months a year — the rare Caribbean cluster that never loses a season.

hero.title: Caribbean × Navier — the ABC islands, by foil
hero.subtitle: Curaçao to Bonaire over the reef in silence, cruise pier to resort and dive site without the diesel shuttle — fast, quiet and zero-emission, below the hurricane belt where the season never stops.
hero.what_we_do_together: We bring a foiling-electric water tier to the Dutch Caribbean — the Curaçao↔Bonaire inter-island spine, intra-island cruise/airport/resort/dive transfers across all three islands, and an aspirational Quanta-LR reach to Aruba. Navier supplies the software-defined fleet, captains and the certification path; the islands' port authorities, resort groups and marine-park authorities bring the quays, the demand and the concession framework. Together we re-platform the ABC trio as one year-round silent waterway.

why_now: The ABC islands are pushing high-value, low-impact tourism exactly as their diesel ferry and resort-shuttle fleets age out and Bonaire's National Marine Park tightens on wake and noise. Inter-island demand is already proven and paid — Divi Divi and EZ Air run the Curaçao↔Bonaire and Curaçao↔Aruba turboprop markets daily — while cruise and stayover arrivals hit record highs (Curaçao 1.57M arrivals 2024; Aruba ~1.2M stopover + ~850K cruise; Bonaire 182K stayover, 43% dive, + 359K cruise). A foiling tier arrives as the demand is proven, the diesel alternative comes under cost and regulatory pressure, and — uniquely — the geography runs all year below the hurricane belt.
multimodal_fit: A foiling vessel meets arrivals at Queen Beatrix (Aruba) and Hato (Curaçao) airport waterfronts and at the Oranjestad, Willemstad and Kralendijk cruise piers, linking the air and cruise gateways to resort strips, marinas and dive sites. The water leg replaces the slowest, least pleasant segment — the diesel shuttle queue, the costly inter-island turboprop, the long dive-boat run — with a fast, silent, scenic run over the reef.

differentiation.why_navier: A foiling-electric premium tier — silent, zero-wake and zero-emission, ideal for Bonaire's marine park and Curaçao's reef zones where diesel craft are least welcome — and software-defined for a fleet that improves over time. Backed by an at-scale operating network already rolling out in the Maldives, the closest analog to the ABC trio's island-and-reef geography. And uniquely below the hurricane belt: a fixed fleet that earns revenue all 12 months.

proof_points.claim: Below the hurricane belt = year-round operability.
proof_points.evidence: The ABC islands sit at ~12°N, south of the main Atlantic hurricane track — while most Caribbean marine networks lose a season, ABC runs 12 months, the rare cluster where a fixed foiling fleet earns revenue all year.

proof_points.claim: The inter-island demand is already proven and paid.
proof_points.evidence: Divi Divi Air (16 flights/day, 19-seat) and EZ Air run the Curaçao↔Bonaire and Curaçao↔Aruba turboprop markets daily — a live, paid substitution pool the foiling network consolidates.

proof_points.claim: Three captive demand engines, not one.
proof_points.evidence: Cruise (Aruba ~850K + Curaçao 834,890 + Bonaire 359,000 pax), stayover resort (Aruba ~1.2M, Curaçao 700K), and dive (Bonaire 43% of stayover into a national marine park) — each a distinct captive transfer pool.

proof_points.claim: Decarbonization and marine-park protection mandate it.
proof_points.evidence: Bonaire National Marine Park enforces zero-wake/silent operation and island diesel grids carry a high carbon baseline — the same regulatory and carbon tailwind that pulls foiling into protected water.
~100 vessels / $100M phased rollout already underway in the Maldives — the closest operating analog to the ABC trio's island-and-reef geography.

objections.concern: Is the inter-island demand beyond cruise transfers real?
objections.response: It's already paid: Divi Divi and EZ Air run daily 19-seat turboprops on Curaçao↔Bonaire and Curaçao↔Aruba. That's a live, priced inter-island market a single silent foiling network consolidates — plus the cruise, resort and dive transfer pools layered on top.

objections.concern: How does it compare to the inter-island flight?
objections.response: On Curaçao↔Bonaire (~38nm), a Pioneer II run is competitive point-to-point, far cheaper than the turboprop, weather-resilient below the hurricane belt, and berths at the town pier and marina rather than a remote airstrip — no transfer at either end.

objections.concern: Noise and wake in Bonaire's marine park?
objections.response: Foiling is near-silent and produces minimal wake at cruise — purpose-built for Bonaire National Marine Park and Curaçao's reef zones, where conventional craft face the tightest restrictions.

objections.concern: Three different regulatory regimes (Aruba, Curaçao, Bonaire)?
objections.response: Aruba and Curaçao are autonomous countries within the Kingdom of the Netherlands; Bonaire is a special municipality of NL using USD. All three sit under a Dutch-Caribbean regulatory umbrella with a clear first-of-class certification path, and the network is sequenced island-by-island to match each concession framework.

phases.label: Phase 1 — the Curaçao hub + intra-island transfers
phases.narrative: Launch on the operational hub — Curaçao — with intra-island cruise/airport/resort transfers (Willemstad, Hato, Spanish Water/Jan Thiel) where cruise and stayover demand is densest and the protected leeward water is calm year-round.
phases.rationale: Start where the demand is densest and the water is most protected: Curaçao's deep-water Spanish Water marina as the operational hub, feeding the cruise pier and resort cluster.

phases.label: Phase 2 — the Curaçao↔Bonaire spine + Bonaire dive/marine-park network
phases.narrative: Open the grounded inter-island spine — Curaçao↔Bonaire (~38nm Pioneer II) — and the Bonaire dive/marine-park transfers (Kralendijk, Klein Bonaire, Harbour Village), consolidating the live turboprop market and the zero-wake dive pool into one silent network.
phases.rationale: The Curaçao↔Bonaire turboprop market is already paid and high-frequency; Bonaire's marine park is the textbook zero-wake showcase.

phases.label: Phase 3 — the full ABC trio + Aruba reach (Quanta-LR)
phases.narrative: Add Aruba's cruise/resort intra-island transfers and the aspirational Quanta-LR reach — Aruba↔Curaçao (~70nm) and Aruba↔Bonaire (~95-100nm) — completing the trio. Long legs are flagged amber-dashed (roadmap) and never faked on a 70nm boat.
phases.rationale: Extend the proven Curaçao-Bonaire network west to Aruba: the hybrid opens the cross-island links a 70nm Pioneer II cannot ground.

the_ask.navier_brings: The software-defined foiling fleet, captains, the maintenance and Dutch-Caribbean certification path, and the network playbook proven in the Maldives.
the_ask.partner_brings: Quay and jetty access (Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire port authorities, resort and marina operators), the demand base, and the local operating, marine-park and concession framework.
the_ask.next_step: A pilot MOU on the Curaçao hub — intra-island cruise/resort transfers — the densest, lowest-risk proof point, with the Curaçao↔Bonaire spine as the fast-follow.

close.title: The Dutch Caribbean trio, re-platformed as one year-round silent waterway.
close.body: Three islands minutes apart by sea, below the hurricane belt, linked today by diesel shuttle and costly turboprop. A foiling-electric tier glides silently over the reef — the Curaçao hub, the Curaçao-Bonaire spine and the reach to Aruba — zero-wake and zero-emission where the marine park and the reefs need it most, and earning every month of the year.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop - roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time. A step-change in marine mobility, not an incremental faster boat.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists - the open ocean and the berths and jetties already in use. No vertiports, no new rights-of-way, no tunnels or tracks. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the Quanta-LR hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Three forces just converged: the technology crossed from prototype to platform (10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out), decarbonization mandates turned legacy diesel fleets into stranded liabilities, and the hybrid removed the 'no charging at the islands' excuse. The marine layer is being claimed cluster-by-cluster right now.
